title: Monogenic Diabetes: MODY (GCK, HNF1A, HNF4A) and Neonatal Diabetes (KCNJ11/ABCC8)
subject: ss-paediatric-endocrinology
module: Type 1 Diabetes, Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Neonatal Hypoglycemia

steps.say: Monogenic diabetes must be actively distinguished from autoimmune diabetes in young non-obese individuals.
steps.tx: Identify characteristic **MODY clinical diagnostic features** indicating single-gene autosomal dominant diabetes. MODY features non-ketotic, non-insulin-dependent diabetes presenting before 25 years of age with autosomal dominant inheritance across >= 3 generations, preserved C-peptide secretion, and absent pancreatic islet autoantibodies. Molecular genetic confirmation provides accurate risk counseling for extended family members and distinguishes these entities from type 1 diabetes.

vis.alt: Cellular diagram of a pancreatic beta cell showing glucose transporter, glucokinase sensor enzyme, and nuclear transcription factors implicated in monogenic diabetes.
vis.caption: Beta-cell glucokinase glucose sensing and transcription factor network disrupted in MODY.

steps.say: Glucokinase mutations reset the glycemic set-point, causing mild stable fasting hyperglycemia without microvascular risk.
steps.tx: Recognize the benign course of **GCK-MODY (MODY 2) set-point defect** across pediatric and adult cohorts. GCK mutations (7p13) alter the pancreatic glucokinase glucose sensor, raising the threshold for insulin secretion; patients demonstrate mild, asymptomatic, stable fasting hyperglycemia (100-145 mg/dL), HbA1c 5.6-7.3%, and do NOT require pharmacotherapy or develop microvascular complications.

right.title: Clinical Management
points: Treatment only considered during pregnancy if fetus unaffected

steps.say: HNF1A mutations cause progressive diabetes with a low renal glucose threshold and exquisite sulfonylurea sensitivity.
steps.tx: Identify the genetics and treatment of **HNF1A-MODY (MODY 3) low renal threshold** in adolescents. HNF1A mutations cause progressive beta-cell dysfunction, low renal glucose threshold (glycosuria at blood glucose < 180 mg/dL), marked sensitivity to low-dose oral sulfonylureas, and cardiovascular risk, managed effectively with gliclazide or glibenclamide.

vis.title: HNF1A-MODY Diagnostic and Management Pathway

nodes.label: Adolescent Diabetes + Glycosuria at BG < 180 mg/dL
Genetic Confirmation of Heterozygous HNF1A Mutation

edges: Replaces insulin in over 80% of cases

steps.say: HNF4A mutations uniquely cause transient hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and macrosomia in neonates.
steps.tx: Recognize the perinatal presentation of **HNF4A-MODY (MODY 1) neonatal macrosomia** in infant carriers. Mutations in HNF4A cause transient hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and macrosomia (> 4 kg birth weight) in neonates, followed in adolescence by progressive non-ketotic diabetes responsive to sulfonylureas such as glibenclamide.

left.title: Neonatal Presentation
points: Marked macrosomia with birth weight > 4 kg
Responsive to diazoxide therapy in infancy

right.title: Adolescent Presentation
points: Highly sensitive to low-dose oral sulfonylureas

steps.say: Any diabetes diagnosed before six months of age is monogenic and mandates urgent genetic testing.
steps.tx: Establish the critical **Neonatal diabetes mellitus (NDM) definition window** for diagnostic decision-making. Diabetes diagnosed before 6 months of age is monogenic in > 85% of cases and is NOT autoimmune type 1 diabetes; testing for KCNJ11 and ABCC8 mutations is urgently indicated to guide therapy.

vis.title: Neonatal Diabetes vs Type 1 Diabetes Distinctions
rows: Extremely rare before 6 months of age
Polygenic HLA class II DR3/DR4 susceptibility

steps.say: Most infants with potassium channel mutations can be successfully transitioned from insulin to high-dose sulfonylureas.
steps.tx: Execute the protocol for **Oral sulfonylurea transition in KCNJ11 NDM** under careful inpatient monitoring. Over 90% of infants with permanent neonatal diabetes caused by activating KCNJ11 or ABCC8 mutations can be successfully transitioned off insulin injections to high-dose oral sulfonylureas (glibenclamide 0.2-1.0 mg/kg/day), binding SUR1 directly to close KATP channels.

vis.title: Inpatient Glibenclamide Transition Protocol

nodes.label: Wean and Cease Subcutaneous Insulin Injections

edges: Over 90% successfully achieve complete insulin independence

steps.say: Severe activating KCNJ11 mutations couple neonatal diabetes with developmental delay and early-onset epilepsy.
steps.tx: Identify the multi-system neurodevelopmental features of the **DEND syndrome spectrum** in affected infants. Severe activating KCNJ11 mutations cause Developmental delay, Epilepsy, and Neonatal Diabetes (DEND syndrome), where high-dose sulfonylureas such as glibenclamide penetrate the blood-brain barrier and improve neurodevelopment. Prompt genetic sequencing enables early targeted pharmacotherapy with high-dose sulfonylureas to improve neurodevelopmental outcomes and seizure frequency.

vis.title: DEND Syndrome Triad and Severity
rows: Open KATP channels in beta cells
Open KATP channels in cortical neurons
Severe developmental delay and infantile epilepsy
Improves both glycemic control and neurological scores

steps.say: Transient neonatal diabetes resolves in early life but carries a substantial risk of relapse during adolescence.
steps.tx: Recognize the genetic etiology and clinical trajectory of **Transient neonatal diabetes (6q24 imprinting)** in infants. Transient NDM resolves spontaneously by 12-18 months of life, caused by overexpression of imprinted genes at 6q24 (paternal uniparental isodisomy or duplication of PLAGL1/HYMAI), though relapsing during puberty into permanent non-ketotic diabetes.

left.title: Infant Phase
points: Onset in first weeks of life with severe IUGR
Insulin required for initial metabolic control

right.title: Adolescent Relapse
points: Recurrence of diabetes during pubertal insulin resistance
Permanent diabetes requiring lifestyle and oral agents
